text: Initial reading: inputs/Q.tex is Bergemann--Koh--Morris on capability and alignment under verifiable actions; inputs/P.tex is a proposal to meter tokens in an LLM double auction, with no combined experiment. I will test whether Q\(\)s implementability restrictions expose a specific failure or design requirement for P\(\)s token tariff, and look for a precise theoretical or experimental result beyond P\(\)s existing proposal.

Critical source mismatch: the assigned Q is Bergemann–Koh–Morris, "Mechanism Design for Alignment and Control" (Q.tex lines 188–211), whereas P.tex lines 13–20 identifies its own Q as Struski et al., "Competitive market behavior of LLMs," and its P as Hansen et al. The auction facts and \(G^{\star}=7.5\) in P.tex lines 22–35 are claims about that other paper, not findings of the assigned Q. I will evaluate the actual Q/P pair and not treat P’s internal source labels as authoritative.

The pair has a potential design connection: assigned Q.tex lines 1660–1725, Proposition \(\ref{prop:full-discipline}\), uses distinct conditional beliefs over peers to elicit unverifiable types with a quadratic score and enforce any feasible action rule. P.tex lines 22–30 gives 11 distinct reservation values per side. If (an added assumption) those values are assigned by a uniform random permutation within each side, a trader with value \(x\) assigns zero probability to a same-side peer having \(x\), and \(1/10\) to each other value. For two different values, the two conditional distributions differ in exactly two coordinates and have squared Euclidean distance \(2/10^2=1/50\). Thus Q\(\)s peer-separation condition can be engineered in P\(\)s laboratory auction, allowing truthful value elicitation and direct efficient matching with token costs, subject to unrestricted transfers, credible enforcement, and the permutation assumption. I am checking whether this gives a useful benchmark rather than merely restating Q.

Tentative bridge: Q.tex lines 1508–1571 permits multi-agent rewards \(R_i\) conditioned on the joint action profile, and lines 2452–2453 says a dynamic trajectory can be an action. P.tex lines 37–47 proposes charging each auction trader’s tokens and notes that crossing may spare the counterparty later calls. A sharpened question is whether a per-trader token tariff leaves a delay externality: in a two-step guaranteed-trade subgame, delay can improve a buyer’s price by \(d\) while burning expected own tokens \(K_B\) and seller tokens \(K_S\). Buyer delays if \(d>\tau K_B\); gross surplus is unchanged, while social net welfare falls by \(\lambda(K_B+K_S)\). This is a candidate incentive wedge, not a result established by either paper; I am checking whether P already states it and whether assumptions can be made credible.

Minimal formal overlap is exact but modest: Q.tex lines 278–294 lets \(A\) contain a complete trajectory; Q.tex lines 1508–1519 allows \(R_i\) to depend on joint actions; Q.tex lines 2452–2453 explicitly notes dynamic trajectories but flags analytic difficulty. Define a trader trajectory’s generated-token total \(C_i(a_i)\), use private tariff \(r_i(a)=-\tau C_i(a_i)\), and replace Q’s human objective by P.tex lines 28–35, \(v_{\lambda}(a,\theta)=G(a,\theta)-\lambda\sum_i C_i(a_i)\). Q’s incentive compatibility then gives a framework to test a specific auction policy. This embedding alone is an application of Q, not a new theorem; P has no data from the assigned Q and reports no combined experiment (P.tex lines 9–11, 53–58).

Limits on the bridge: P.tex lines 37–41 already states qualitatively that a trader charged for its own calls ignores a counterparty’s possible saving, so the simple delay wedge is a formalization, not by itself a novel result. Q’s coupled-reward proposition at lines 1862–1882 solves a quadratic simultaneous-action model under a strong curve restriction on hidden biases; it does not establish an auction transfer. Q’s single-agent cycle characterization (lines 522–664) is state-independent and cannot simply be cited as an implementability theorem for a sequential multi-trader auction. Applying Q requires observable token counts, a trajectory/action encoding, specified beliefs and rational response; P.tex lines 53–58 leaves token-record reliability and charge comprehension unresolved.

Conditional two-step result for a possible Q/P paper: at a P-style order-book history, crossing now trades a fixed pair with buyer margin \(m=v-p\) and gross gain \(g=v-c>0\). Waiting yields the same match with probability \(q\), an expected buyer price concession \(\delta\) conditional on trade, and incremental expected future tokens \(K_B,K_S\geq0\); assume no trade otherwise and no other gross effect. With private per-token tariff \(\tau\), the buyer crosses iff \((1-q)m+\tau K_B\geq q\delta\). The social difference (cross minus wait) is \((1-q)g+\lambda(K_B+K_S)>0\) whenever \(q<1\) or extra tokens are positive. Thus a region with \(q\delta>(1-q)m+\tau K_B\) exhibits private waiting despite higher net social value from crossing. This deduction formalizes P.tex lines 37–47 using P’s \(G,C,W_{\lambda}\) (lines 22–35), and suggests using Q.tex lines 1508–1519’s joint-action-contingent rewards to test a crossing incentive. It is conditional on optimizing behavior, same-match continuation, and unknown \(q,\delta,K_B,K_S\); no claimed effect in actual LLM runs. An efficient reward must also address the price-transfer motive \(q\delta\), so merely rebating the counterparty’s token cost can be insufficient.

The permutation/peer-score bridge in entry 3 is mathematically valid only after adding uniform random assignment within each side. P.tex line 23 lists distinct values but does not state that assignment is random, and Q.tex Proposition \(\ref{prop:full-discipline}\) relies on unrestricted transfers and an \(-\infty\) off-support prohibition. A direct-report mechanism would also replace P\(\)s standing-book rules, so this is at best a cost benchmark, not an explanation of P\(\)s proposed tariff experiment. I am prioritizing a within-mechanism revealed-price restriction instead.

Cross-check of emmy #3/#8 against Q.tex lines 1650–1715: \(1/50\) is the squared \(\ell_2\) separation for the marginal value of one randomly selected same-side peer under the added uniform-permutation assumption. Q’s \(\beta_i[t_i]\) is instead the distribution over the entire co-player type profile. With 10 labeled same-side peers and 11 labeled opposite-side peers permuted independently, supports for two distinct own values are disjoint and the full-profile squared separation is \(2/(10!\,11!)\), not \(1/50\). A modified peer score that samples or projects to one same-side report could recover \(1/50\), but it would be a separate construction. The qualitative separation and emmy’s benchmark caveat stand.

My current judgment: preserve the assigned pairing and foreground the source mismatch (#2). The strongest viable lead is a narrow auction subgame theorem plus an experiment comparing P’s uniform token tariff with a Q-style history/joint-action-contingent crossing incentive. The theorem in #7 is conditional and mostly sharpens P’s own qualitative claim, so I would not present it alone as publication-ready. Unresolved: derive incentive-compatible rewards under private values and preserved standing-book rules; estimate continuation trade probability, price concessions and incremental tokens; test whether LLM traders actually respond to charges. I do not infer auction results from the assigned Q or claim a positive empirical effect.

A distinct, testable Q/P bridge is in emmy/revealed_price_test.md. Q.tex lines 278–294 and 2450–2453 allow a full response trajectory as an action; lines 319–404 use additive rewards and obedience inequalities. P.tex lines 37–47 proposes a disclosed token tariff but has no run. At a fixed trader type/book state/opponent policy/common feasible set, suppose action \(a\) has stable expected payoff \(U(a)\), metered tokens \(T(a)\), and the charge is actual additive reward \(-\tau T(a)\). If \(a_j\) is optimal at \(\tau_0<\tau_1\), adding the two optimality inequalities gives \((\tau_1-\tau_0)(T(a_0)-T(a_1))\geq0\), hence \(T(a_1)\leq T(a_0)\). This also holds for optimal lotteries in expectation. Therefore a fixed-snapshot price randomization yields a necessary revealed-preference test before interpreting P\(\)s full-auction treatment as a cost response. No sign follows for spread crossing, withdrawals, or total run tokens; a changed order book invalidates the fixed-state comparison. This is a new diagnostic, not a direct corollary of Q\(\)s cycle theorem or an observed effect.
ready at #10

Ada #9 correctly distinguishes the marginal peer calculation from Q\(\)s full-profile score. I revised emmy/revealed_price_test.md to state that \(1/50\) is the separation for one selected same-side peer and would require a modified score; it is not Q\(\)s full-profile separation. This does not affect the main two-price result.

Cross-check of emmy #11 and emmy/revealed_price_test.md: its two optimality inequalities and bound \(T(a_1)\leq T(a_0)\) for \(\tau_1>\tau_0\) are algebraically correct when \(U,T,A\) are stable across prices; the payoff-difference interval is also correct. This seems the best concrete use of Q’s additive-reward/obedience logic (Q.tex lines 319–404) for P’s unrun disclosed tariff (P.tex lines 37–47). It is an elementary necessary restriction, not a new theorem about auctions or LLMs. P’s live-auction aggregate tokens can increase because opponent behavior, book states and participation change; my #7 delay wedge explains one reason private token demand and social stopping incentives diverge. The fixed-state test should be the diagnostic before claiming any auction-level price response. Observed violations would reject joint stability/optimization/metering assumptions, not identify which one failed.
ready at #14

Identification limit for my #11: Q.tex lines 319–343 and 348–404 define an actual additive reward in the agent\(\)s payoff and require obedience under it. P.tex line 42 proposes a charge in each trader\(\)s stated payoff, while line 54 explicitly leaves charge comprehension unresolved. Therefore a prompt announcing \(\tau\) does not establish the premise that choices maximize stable \(U(a)-\tau T(a)\). The two-price inequality is a falsifiable joint restriction under that premise; a violation can reflect prompt-sensitive preferences, altered beliefs, inaccessible/hidden tokens, or nonoptimization. A pass is only necessary, and full-auction totals have no monotonic prediction.

Targeted prior-work check for the fixed-state diagnostic: queries were "arxiv LLM agents inference token cost price demand revealed preference experiment tokens", "arxiv large language models price sensitivity token usage revealed preference", and "site:arxiv.org/abs token price revealed preference LLM agents". Relevant adjacent work includes token-budget prompting at https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.18547 and language-model revealed-preference tests at https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26288. These results limit any broad novelty claim; I found no evidence in this targeted search that the exact Q/P fixed-book tariff diagnostic has been run, but this is not an exhaustive claim.
ready at #17

Conditional counterexample strengthening #7 and limiting #11: At a fixed standing-book history, a buyer can cross the seller ask \(p\) now or post a bid \(p-\delta\), where \(v>p>p-\delta>c\). Assume both initial responses use the same metered buyer tokens; if the buyer bids, a later scheduled seller call crosses that bid with certainty, uses \(K_S>0\) additional seller tokens, and requires no further buyer call. The match and gross gain \(v-c\) are identical. For every own-token tariff \(\tau\geq0\), the buyer strictly prefers the bid, gaining \(\delta>0\) in price with no change in its token charge. Yet for every social conversion \(\lambda>0\), crossing now raises \(W_{\lambda}\) by \(\lambda K_S\). Thus a uniform own-token tariff cannot generally implement the welfare-best crossing even if traders perfectly optimize the stated charge; the problem is an unpriced counterparty call plus a price-transfer motive. This is a conditional possibility, not a prediction of actual runs. It uses P.tex lines 29–39 on \(G,C,W_{\lambda}\) and avoided counterparty calls, while Q.tex lines 1508–1519 permits joint-action-contingent rewards that could in principle target the history. No implementability claim follows without verifiable histories, values or suitable reports, and transfer feasibility. Emmy #16 is correct that a disclosed prompt may not instantiate the additive payoff premise in the first place.

Clarification to #19: the phrase "for every \(\tau\)" needs an explicit continuation incentive. Assume the seller's next call is imposed by the scheduler if the buyer bids, its metered cost \(K_S\) is the same whether it accepts that bid or declines, and \(p-\delta>c\). Conditional on that call, accepting strictly dominates declining for the seller at every \(\tau\), because the call charge cancels. The buyer's two initial replies also have equal metered tokens. These assumptions make #19 a sequentially rational local counterexample even with an actual additive tariff. They are stringent and should be tested against the operative auction scheduler and reply metering; without them, a sufficiently high tariff could deter the seller's later trade and undo the claimed all-\(\tau\) statement.

Cross-check of ada #19: the buyer comparison is valid when its two initial responses use the same metered tokens and the seller certainly crosses the posted bid. The quantifier \(\tau\geq0\) needs that continuation to remain fixed as \(\tau\) varies. If the seller can avoid the future call or declines a net-negative trade, large tariffs can destroy certain continuation; P.tex lines 42–47 explicitly changes participation and calls. A clean variant makes the seller call mandatory and its metering sunk before its choice, with \(p-\delta>c\), so crossing then beats declining for every \(\tau\), conditional on equal tokens for either seller response. This is a stylized subgame, not a prediction for P\(\)s random finite auction. Q.tex lines 1508–1525 permits joint-action rewards but does not prove implementation under P\(\)s private values or standing-book protocol.

A concrete Q-style repair for the local counterexample: Let the buyer's intrinsic charged payoff on a trading trajectory \(a\) be \(v-p(a)-\tau C_B(a)\). On histories where the same buyer and seller trade under either feasible continuation, offer a verifiable trajectory-contingent correction \(R_B(a)=p(a)-\lambda C_S(a)-(\lambda-\tau)C_B(a)\). Then its total payoff becomes \(v-\lambda[C_B(a)+C_S(a)]\), so with the match fixed the buyer chooses the lower-token continuation and crosses in #19. The \(p(a)\) term cancels the private price-transfer motive; the \(C_S\) term internalizes the seller's avoided call. Merely making the buyer pay for both agents' tokens leaves the price motive and fails when \(\delta>\lambda K_S\). Q.tex lines 1508–1519 allows rewards conditional on joint actions and Q.tex lines 2452–2453 permits full trajectories, while P.tex lines 29–39 supplies token welfare and the crossing externality. This is a restricted local construction, not a claim that the full auction is implemented: other matches require seller costs and outside options, prices and token counts must be verifiable, the correction may require a funded transfer, and multiple equilibria may remain. A potentially publishable comparison is P's own-token tariff versus this pre-specified corrected reward, after the fixed-snapshot diagnostic in emmy #11; empirical benefit is unknown.

Synthesis and local derivation added to emmy/revealed_price_test.md. The two-price restriction in #11 checks whether a trader behaves as though an actual additive \(-\tau T\) enters a fixed decision problem (Q.tex lines 319–404; P.tex lines 41–47); it is necessary but says nothing by itself about welfare. Ada #19/#20 supplies a complementary conditional limit: with equal buyer reply tokens, a mandatory later seller call of \(K_S>0\), equal seller metering whether it accepts or declines, and \(v>p>p-\delta>c\), the seller accepts at its sunk-cost call, the buyer posts \(p-\delta\) for a private gain \(\delta\) at every \(\tau\geq0\), and immediate crossing would raise \(W_\lambda\) by \(\lambda K_S\) for \(\lambda>0\). Thus a tariff can pass the fixed-state demand test while failing to price a counterparty delay externality. P.tex lines 37–39 already mentions the omitted counterparty saving, so the derivation sharpens rather than invents it; Q.tex lines 1508–1525 permits profile-dependent rewards but gives no auction implementation theorem. Publication would require an actual metered intervention and comparison with a specified, credible history-dependent incentive. Style gate and artifact ban pass for the note.

Current judgment and sharpened question: I changed the focus from "does a tariff reduce tokens or induce crossing?" to "when does own-token pricing fail to induce cost-aware crossing, and can a verifiable joint-trajectory reward repair that failure?" The best supported line is the conditional local counterexample #19–#21 plus correction #22, paired with emmy #11's fixed-state revealed-price diagnostic. P.tex lines 37–47 already anticipates an unpriced counterparty saving, so the theoretical observation alone is not publication-ready; Q.tex lines 1508–1519 and 2452–2453 justify the reward form but not full auction implementation. A publication would need a runnable fixed-book intervention, evidence that stated charges enter behavior, measured seller-call savings and surplus, and a comparison of own-token tariffs with a pre-specified corrected reward under the same values and rules. Assigned Q is Bergemann–Koh–Morris, while P.tex lines 13–20 uses its own Q/P labels for other papers, as #2 records. Unresolved: whether P's operative scheduler and token meter support #19's assumptions, whether the reward can be credibly funded and observed, how to handle private values and changed matches, and whether any empirical effect exists. I do not claim novelty from the targeted prior-work search in emmy #17.
ready at #24

Cross-check of ada #22: the proposed reward \(R_B(a)=p(a)-\lambda C_S(a)-(\lambda-\tau)C_B(a)\) algebraically changes the buyer payoff \(v-p(a)-\tau C_B(a)\) into \(v-\lambda[C_B(a)+C_S(a)]\) on fixed-match trajectories. Hence it repairs the local #19 example if prices and both token totals are verifiable and the reward is actually implemented. Charging only both token totals still leaves a price motive: in the example the buyer waits if \(\delta>\lambda K_S\). I added the derivation to emmy/revealed_price_test.md and reran both style gates successfully. Caveat: reimbursing \(p(a)\) may require an external subsidy, and neither Q.tex lines 1508–1519 nor P.tex lines 37–47 proves a budget-feasible incentive-compatible rule for changing matches and private values.
